lesson.title: Indentured Servitude: Bound Labor and the Price of Passage
lesson.summary: Indentured servitude bound poor English migrants to years of unpaid labor in exchange for passage to America, supplying the workforce that the headright system rewarded planters for importing, before the institution gave way to racial slavery.
lesson.body:
For most of the seventeenth century, the majority of European migrants who crossed the Atlantic to the Chesapeake colonies did not pay their own way. Instead they signed an indenture, a legal contract binding them to work for a master for a fixed term, typically four to seven years, in exchange for the cost of their passage plus food, clothing, and shelter during their service. Historians estimate that well over half of all English immigrants to Virginia and Maryland during the 1600s arrived under some form of this arrangement. Most were young, poor, and unmarried, drawn from England's crowded cities and depressed rural counties by the hope of eventually owning land of their own.

The system connected directly to the headright system that Virginia had adopted in 1618. Because planters received fifty acres of land for every servant whose passage they paid, servitude became not just a source of labor but a source of land itself. A planter with enough capital to transport a shipload of servants could accumulate hundreds of acres almost overnight, which meant the demand for indentured workers stayed high throughout the century, especially as tobacco cultivation expanded and required more hands to plant, weed, and harvest.

Life as an indentured servant was hard and often short. Servants could be bought, sold, or transferred like other property for the length of their contract, though unlike enslaved people their bondage was not hereditary and did have a defined end. Masters could legally extend a servant's term for infractions like running away or bearing a child out of wedlock, and mortality from disease, especially in the swampy, disease prone Chesapeake, was high enough that many servants never lived to see freedom. Those who survived their term were owed what were called freedom dues, which might include clothing, tools, a small amount of corn, and in the earliest decades sometimes even land, though the value of these dues shrank considerably as the century went on and free land became scarcer.

By the middle of the seventeenth century, a growing population of former servants, now free but often landless and struggling, created social tension in Virginia that boiled over in Bacon's Rebellion in 1676. That uprising, in which former servants and small farmers joined together against the colonial government, alarmed Virginia's elite planters and made clear the dangers of a large class of poor, resentful freemen. In the decades that followed, planters increasingly turned away from indentured servitude and toward enslaved African labor, which offered a permanent, hereditary workforce that could never legally claim freedom or demand land of its own. Indentured servitude did not disappear immediately, but its central role in the colonial labor system steadily declined as slavery expanded.
